## Executive Summary


The €645,000 fine imposed on the HSE by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) shows that paper records carry the same regulatory exposure as any digital system. The agency issued a reprimand and imposed corrective orders over the insecure storage of paper medical records. The HSE accepted the findings and apologised. First and foremost, this affected patients whose sensitive records were exposed, and our thoughts are with them. This article outlines a practical route from costly storage to governed, accessible information for organisations that still hold legacy paper records.


## Paper Is Personal Data Too


During the 23 years I spent in the NHS, I saw the same records risk repeated. Most healthcare organisations treat data security as a digital problem; yet many sensitive, personal healthcare records sit in paper files. The DPC’s recent decision raised several critical questions:


- Are we ignoring the security of sensitive data just because it lives on paper?
- How do we enforce genuine data protection across legacy archives?
- How do we stop holding expired patient files, when €300,000 of this fine was for keeping records longer than necessary?


Legacy healthcare records are a risk many organisations still haven’t confronted. This article sets out a route from unmanaged paper archives to secure, governed, and auditable records, drawing on 23 years in the NHS, spanning outpatient services, large digital portfolios, health records digitisation and advising NHS England on outpatient and health records transformation.


## The Overlooked Archive


Many organisations still treat GDPR as a digital issue. Effort concentrates on systems, networks and cybersecurity, while the paper archive receives far less attention. Unmanaged paper records are an active regulatory, reputational, and patient safety risk, not simply a legacy filing issue. If a record contains personal data, the same duties apply whether it sits in a database or a box file. A digital system can show who accessed a record and when. A storage room cannot. Without an access log and regular checks on the building, an organisation may not know a record has been lost, damaged or viewed until someone else tells them.


## What This Means for NHS Trusts


The same principles apply in the UK under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, overseen by the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). For NHS bodies, the bigger exposure may not be a fine: a published ICO reprimand, a weaker Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) assertion, or questions at a CQC well-led inspection all carry real reputational cost. The NHS Records Management Code of Practice sets clear retention schedules, and boards are expected to show they are being followed.


The risks go well beyond regulation:


- **Patient safety:** missing or incomplete notes in clinic delay decisions, lead to repeat tests and leave clinicians working without the full picture.
- **Cost:** off-site storage, retrieval and courier charges rise every year, and the estate used for on-site records libraries is space that could be used for patient care.
- **Physical and staff safety:** records held in ageing or disused buildings are exposed to fire, flood, damp and contamination, and the staff who retrieve them are exposed too.
- **Visibility:** without an index and an access log, a trust cannot say with confidence what it holds, who has seen it, or whether anything is missing.


## The Cost of Keeping Records Longer


The €300,000 penalty for keeping records longer than necessary matched the penalty for security failings. Storage limitation is the principle most often overlooked. Retention schedules exist, but records are rarely reviewed, and disposal is seen as risky, costly, or somebody else’s responsibility. In NHS trusts, the pattern is familiar: records are sent offsite ‘just in case’, the storage bill grows every year, and the risk grows with it. Then, when the trust finally digitises, it pays again: retrieval and permanent-withdrawal charges to bring the records back before they can be scanned. In many cases, the better route is to stop sending records off-site and make full use of the scanning capacity and electronic document management (EDM) systems trusts already own. Every record kept beyond its retention period adds cost and exposure without adding value. A growing archive also makes it harder to say with confidence what is held, where, and why.


## Lessons Learned: Know What Your Organisation Holds


Fixing data security starts with knowing what the organisation holds in its archive, where it is, and how long the organisation needs it. An accurate baseline helps the organisation better plan its healthcare records governance in the long run. The DPC’s corrective orders translate into five practical questions for any off-site archive:


1. Have we audited what we hold?
2. Are our sites fit for purpose?
3. Is every record indexed?
4. Does every record series have a retention rule, and is it applied?
5. Is disposal controlled and evidenced?


Disposal must also respect any legal holds or inquiry-related restrictions on destroying records, so the aim is to dispose of what the organisation is permitted to, and to evidence every decision.


Addressing these five questions now is the difference between defensible governance and waiting for an audit or a breach to expose the gaps.


## Digitisation as the Foundation of Electronic Patient Records


Ireland’s Health Minister linked the problem to paper-based records and said a move to electronic health records would fix much of it. Digitisation provides the essential foundation for true electronic healthcare. Converting paper archives into digital assets bridges the divide between physical estate risk and modern clinical workflows. In fact, XBP Europe has a proven track record of transforming historic civil registration records dating back to 1837 for the General Register Office (GRO), with all data processed and securely hosted in the UK.


## Make Records Accessible, Searchable, and Auditable


AI-assisted digitisation converts legacy healthcare records into structured, searchable digital assets. AI automatically classifies documents, speeds up indexing, extracts the key data needed for retention decisions, and makes historic records usable for clinical audit and research. Retention rules can be embedded directly into digital metadata, supporting compliance with storage limitation requirements and creating auditable access logs for every file access.


XBP Europe provides an end-to-end service:


- secure collection and logistics with full chain of custody;
- on-site or off-site scanning, including working with a trust’s existing scanners and EDM;
- indexing, quality assurance and AI-assisted classification;
- integration with the trust’s EPR or EDM, so records appear in clinicians’ normal workflow;
- retention rules applied in metadata, with certified, evidenced destruction of originals where permitted;
- scan-on-demand and day-forward scanning so the backlog does not return.


XBP Europe operates to recognised information security and quality standards, including ISO/IEC 27001, Cyber Essentials Plus and BS 10008, the British Standard on the legal admissibility of electronic records.


I have seen these results first-hand in the programmes I led during my NHS career:


- **Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust:** At Luton and Dunstable University Hospital, the programme digitised more than 7.5 million records, generating approximately £1.16 million in annual recurring benefit and converting former records storage into a modern Cardiac Cath Lab.
- **Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust:** The model was scaled to digitise more than 12 million records, securing approximately £2.15 million in recurring annual benefit and releasing prime hospital space for an Oncology Outpatients department and a TIA One-Stop Scanning and Outpatient facility.


Experience of delivering these programmes shows that digitisation is far more than a defensive compliance exercise. It provides a repeatable model to secure patient data, reduce or remove off-site storage costs, and return critical hospital estate directly to patient care.


## Next Steps for Healthcare Leaders


Healthcare boards cannot afford to treat physical archive governance as an administrative afterthought until regulators force their hand. The recent incident should serve as an urgent prompt for healthcare leaders to confront unmanaged liabilities held in off-site stores. And this doesn’t need to start from scratch. Proven frameworks exist that combine national-scale processing with deep NHS operational pedigree.
